blocks.text: Report an Error Without Returning an Invalid Result

An error signal such as -1 can distinguish an error from a valid result if every caller checks it. Another policy uses exceptions: when a function detects that it cannot fulfill its contract, it throws an object with throw instead of returning normally. Code that knows how to handle the failure can catch it in a catch handler associated with a try block. The mechanism separates detection from handling, but we still need to decide what recovery means.

std::invalid_argument, from <stdexcept>, is a standard-library exception type for an invalid argument. std::invalid_argument{"Invalid quantity"} constructs an object with a diagnostic message. It is not a function from the book's support library. Standard-library types let us explore this idea before designing our own classes. In the prediction exercises, we show fixed messages from catch; we do not depend on compiler-specific internal wording.

The valid call returns 7, that result is printed, and catch is skipped. If an exception is thrown inside try, subsequent statements in that try are skipped until a compatible handler is found. The const reference in catch lets us inspect the object without modifying it. The variable name error does not require us to print the exception object; here we use a message from our domain.

blocks.text: A Compatible catch and a Policy for What Comes Next

A catch must recognize the thrown type or an appropriate, more general exception type. If no calling function catches an exception that escapes main, the program terminates through the C++ termination mechanism. Do not use that termination as a recovery strategy. In the course labs, we catch the failures we deliberately trigger.

blocks.text: Build and Check Both Execution Paths

Use the default Clang 23 compiler to practice throw/catch; the alternative Clang 21 does not support this exercise. The input values are prepared in the code; change the indicated values before running it.

Predict and run the code with piezas set to 0, 3, and 11. Add the text Before before the call and After after the call inside try. Keep End outside try/catch. Explain which outputs are missing when the value is invalid and which ones remain. Do not try to trigger errors by dividing by zero, accessing an invalid index with [], or causing overflow.
Consult this comparison after building and testing your attempt. It is one possible implementation; other solutions are valid if they meet the same contract and the stated criteria.

Correctness criteria. With the concatenated messages from this reference, 0 produces Before0After:End, 3 produces Before9After:End, and 11 produces BeforeInvalid:End. Before is preserved because it was printed before the call; After and the normal result are missing if the call throws. End is preserved outside try/catch. Another separator format is acceptable if the same stages are identifiable and the exceptional path remains visible.

Change only piezas to compare the three paths. Catching the exception allows execution to reach End; it does not retry the call or return to the following statement inside the abandoned try. The function rejects invalid values before calculating, and all deliberately triggered failures have compatible handlers.
